cases.title: Logbaba gas project and the Ndogpassi neighbourhoods
cases.point: The Logbaba gas site in the Ndogpassi area of eastern Douala, with the Ndogpassi I, II and III neighbourhoods around it. 100Reporters places the plant in the Ndogpassi neighbourhood of east Douala; the complainants are the residents' association of Ndogpassi I, II and III.

lenders.name: Victoria Oil and Gas plc (United Kingdom), through Gaz du Cameroun S.A. (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Wholly owns Gaz du Cameroun, which holds 57% of the Logbaba project and operates it. RSM Production Company holds 38% and Cameroon's Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures 5%.

cases.conditions: No outside lender was found; the money was the operator's own, under a concession in which the state oil company holds 5%. The only conditions on the record are the ones the UK NCP later found unmet: no system to engage the local population, and no contingency plan for preventing or controlling serious environmental and health damage from the operations.

companies.name: Victoria Oil and Gas plc
companies.desc: UK-registered oil and gas company whose main asset is the Logbaba field in Douala.

companies.name: Gaz du Cameroun S.A.
companies.role: Operator of the Logbaba gas and condensate field
companies.desc: Victoria Oil and Gas's Cameroonian subsidiary. Gas is carried through a 34 km pipeline network to four main industrial hubs in the region (Offshore Technology). The company told the UK contact point it had about 128 employees during 2017, 97% of them Cameroonians; those are its own figures.

cases.community: 100Reporters found that during construction the company's trucks damaged community water wells. In March 2012 the company dug a replacement well, spending about $25,000; Chief Antoine Tebu said it was not drilled deep enough to reach clean water, and residents described a foul smell and yellow staining. One resident, Frank Tchinda, 23, said: "You would have to be blind to not see that this water is bad." The company and the government said the water had been tested at the Pasteur Centre laboratory. The complainants' own survey, recorded by the UK NCP, found 81.70% of respondents had experienced noise from the site and 31.60% complained of odours, and they alleged vibrations had cracked the walls of 23 houses, supplying a proximity map and photographs of soil erosion. Victoria Oil and Gas admitted that on one occasion in September 2017 it failed to warn the local community before flaring. Compensation for houses inside the safety zone was assessed by a commission set up by the Senior Divisional Officer for Wouri; the company said its subsidiary was not part of that commission.
cases.ecosystem: Pasteur Centre reports supplied by the complainants described the water quality as "unsatisfactory and mediocre". The environmental consultant the UK NCP commissioned concluded that none of the documents provided made a compelling case for assigning responsibility to the site, while also finding that the company had left itself open to complaints by not setting a detailed water-quality baseline.
cases.suppression: 100Reporters reports that soldiers of Cameroon's Rapid Intervention Battalion (BIR) were posted at the facility from late 2013. Chief Tebu and a resident, Alain Tedom, 28, described beatings of moto-taxi drivers and their passengers and moto-taxis being barred from the area. On 4 July 2016 a BIR soldier kicked in the door of a garage near the plant, threatened the employees and tried to stab an office worker; the incident was reported to the authorities and to Gaz du Cameroun without response.
cases.outcome: The UK NCP accepted the case on 20 December 2018. Both sides accepted mediation, held one meeting on 30 January 2020, then told the NCP they were pursuing an agreement outside the process; in May 2020 they said they could not reach one, and the NCP began a further examination on 7 May 2020. Its final statement of 22 October 2022 determined that the company did not meet Chapter II paragraphs 7 and 14 on meaningful stakeholder engagement and self-regulatory systems, or Chapter VI paragraphs 5 and 6 on contingency planning and improving environmental performance: materials were not provided in an accessible language, the local population was not given enough time in consultation, and platform meetings were cancelled without notice. It found the company did meet its obligations under the disclosure chapter, the human rights chapter and parts of the employment and environment chapters, and reached no conclusion on three employment paragraphs and two environment paragraphs because there was not enough evidence to substantiate them. It found no infringement of the rights to water, to a healthy environment or to decent housing because the link to the site was not established on the evidence available, while also stating that it is apparent that the local population have experienced negative impacts from the project. It recommended the company build engagement systems, keep improving environmental performance and maintain contingency plans, and said it would report back in September 2023.
cases.whole: Production started in December 2011. Offshore Technology records output of 14.59 million standard cubic feet a day from two wells, original proven and probable reserves of 209.6 billion cubic feet of gas and 2.93 million barrels of condensate, about 202.3 billion cubic feet and 2.83 million barrels remaining as of June 2016, gas piped 34 km to four industrial hubs around Douala, condensate sent to the Sonara refinery at Limbe, and a $40 million two-well drilling programme. The figures for what the project gave the neighbourhood are the company's own, reported to the UK NCP and not independently checked: about 128 employees in 2017, 97% of them Cameroonian, $176,000 invested in local staff training since 2011, and an annual amount for training Cameroon nationals under its contract with the state oil company which stood at $165,000 as of 2018.

sources.title: Cameroon communities vs. Victoria Oil and Gas
Final statement: AHN and CBVL complaint to the UK NCP about Victoria Oil & Gas plc (VOG)

cases.confidence_note: The damaged wells, the replacement well and the beatings by soldiers posted at the plant are documented by 100Reporters, outside the complaint. The pollution itself is not established: the UK NCP's own consultant found the documents did not make a compelling case for assigning responsibility to the site, and the company and the government cite Pasteur Centre tests finding the water acceptable, while the complainants cite Pasteur Centre reports calling it unsatisfactory and mediocre. The UK NCP found non-compliance on engagement and on environmental management systems but no infringement of the rights to water, health or housing. The soldiers were state forces; no source opened here records who requested their deployment. The ownership figures differ between the documents opened: the UK contact point states that Victoria Oil and Gas wholly owns Gaz du Cameroun, which has a 57% interest in the project, and Offshore Technology gives Gaz du Cameroun 57%, RSM Production Company 38% and Societe Nationale des Hydrocarbures 5%, while 100Reporters reports Gaz du Cameroun itself as jointly owned, 55% by Victoria Oil and Gas or its subsidiary, 40% by RSM and 5% by the Cameroonian government. The NCP also stated, alongside its finding of no infringement, that it is apparent the local population have experienced negative impacts from the project.

cases.title: La Platosa mine and the Ejido La Sierrita contract
cases.place: Ejido La Sierrita de Galeana, Tlahualilo, Durango, Mexico
cases.point: The La Platosa silver, lead and zinc mine, on land rented from the Ejido La Sierrita de Galeana. Red TDT and MiningWatch Canada both place the ejido in Tlahualilo municipality, Durango. Excellon's 2016 annual information form puts the property about 45 km north of Torreon, 63 km by road from Torreon airport along Highway 49, with a company warehouse in Bermejillo, and describes the 1,100 hectares rented in 2008 as exploration ground west and northwest of the mine. No source gives the mine's own coordinates, so the point is approximate.

lenders.name: Excellon Resources Inc. (Canada), through Excellon de México S.A. de C.V. (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Leased 1,100 hectares of ejido land under a temporary occupation contract signed on 6 April 2008 and mined La Platosa through the dispute. Red TDT records that from 2008 to 2012 the company met the contract's money clauses but not its social and environmental ones.

cases.conditions: The conditions here were the community's, written into the land contract, not a lender's. The 6 April 2008 temporary occupation contract covered 1,100 hectares for 5.5 million pesos a year adjusted annually for inflation, and required a water treatment plant, hiring preference for ejido members, ejido administration of the workers' canteen and of ore transport, school scholarships and a social fund. Four years earlier, in 2004, the company had taken 27 hectares for 30 years for a single payment of 1.2 million pesos; Red TDT records that what the ejidatarios agreed to was 4 hectares for that price and that the contract they signed said 27 hectares for the same money, after company representatives told them the land was worth nothing and threatened to have it expropriated. Red TDT records that from 2008 to 2012 only the rent, the social fund and the scholarships were delivered, and that on 11 March 2011 the company explored outside the 1,100 hectares without the ejido assembly's authorisation.

companies.name: Excellon Resources Inc.
companies.role: Owner and operator of the La Platosa mine
companies.desc: Canadian mining and exploration company; its 2016 annual information form describes it as focused on silver, lead and zinc on a 20,947-hectare property in northeastern Durango, with its principal office at 20 Victoria Street, Toronto.

cases.community: The ejido assembly voted on 8 July 2012 to blockade the mine entrance, and more than seventy landowners did so, after the company cancelled a 6 July meeting that followed nearly eight months of attempts to settle the breaches. On 11 July 2012 MiningWatch Canada reported that Excellon had threatened the landowners and their legal advisers with criminal proceedings and judicial action, calling the blockade illegal and saying state and federal governments would intervene within 24 to 48 hours. On 29 August 2012 about 100 federal police, soldiers, state police and Mapimí municipal police tried to break up the protest, citing a labour inspection of the mine; the protest carried on and the company resumed normal operations. On 24 October 2012, at about 6:30 in the morning, around 250 men from a mining union, brought from Zacatecas and Chihuahua and carrying sticks and stones, cleared the protest camp; Red TDT records that Robert Moore, Excellon's director of operations, ordered the camp torn down and burned using machinery belonging to La Platosa, and that a criminal complaint filed on 18 December 2012 alleges mine personnel tried, on managers' orders, to run protesters down with heavy machinery. MiningWatch Canada visited the demolished camp on 3 December 2012 and reported that company workers destroyed it in late October in the presence of Excellon's chief operating officer, and that mining equipment was used to bulldoze and burn it. By November 2016, Proceso reported, the company had not paid the rent for three years and had not stopped mining.
cases.suppression: The 29 August 2012 police and army operation to clear the protest; the destruction and burning of the protest camp on 24 October 2012; and the detention, in November 2013, of six community members and relatives of ejidatarios in the days before a court hearing - Héctor Pacheco four days before, and Omar Pacheco, Adolfo Gómez Chareo, Julio Orona, Luis Orona and Ricardo Calderón two days before. Red TDT describes these detentions as arbitrary.
cases.outcome: In November 2012 the Mexican NCP closed the complaint, finding the issues material but not substantiated and citing Excellon's unwillingness to take part in any mediation; the complainants said the threshold for acceptance was unreasonably high and that the Canadian NCP appears not to have been involved at all. In 2011 Canada's Office of the Extractive Sector CSR Counsellor had received a complaint on the same facts, carried out an investigation including a field visit, and concluded the request should go straight to structured dialogue; Excellon withdrew before dialogue began. The ejido went to court instead: on 4 September 2012 it sued for rescission of the contract, restitution of the land and damages (file 683/2012, Tribunal Unitario Agrario del Distrito Sexto, Torreón). Evidence was heard on 23 January 2014. On 7 August 2014 the Juzgado Tercero de Distrito en La Laguna granted an amparo filed on 18 December 2013 (case 2489/2013), ordering the agrarian tribunal to issue a new ruling recognising the ejidatarios' rights and holding that the withheld rent caused the ejido community irreparable harm; the company appealed. A criminal complaint for ecological damage filed on 18 December 2012 produced no investigation. As of 30 November 2014 the tribunal had still not released the rent and the contract remained in force. On 10 November 2016 the ejido filed a further amparo over the delay, seven months after case 683/2012 had been sent for judgment with no ruling issued. Excellon's own annual information form records that the ruling came on 16 November 2016: the Agrarian Tribunal rescinded the contract on the company's application, awarded Excellon 5.5 million pesos against the ejido for losses from what it called an illegal blockade, and awarded the ejido 5.5 million pesos against Excellon as indemnity for not building the water treatment plant, the two awards setting off against each other so that neither side had to pay. The company said it was considering next steps on the award to the ejido, on the ground that building the plant depended on conditions the ejido never met, including obtaining a water use permit.
cases.whole: Excellon's own figures for Platosa output are 1.2 million ounces of silver, 7.5 million pounds of lead and 10.1 million pounds of zinc in 2014; 0.8 million ounces of silver, 4.4 million pounds of lead and 7.4 million pounds of zinc in 2015; and 0.8 million ounces of silver, 4.4 million pounds of lead and 5.6 million pounds of zinc in 2016. These are self-reported in the company's annual information form. Of what the 2008 contract promised the ejido, Red TDT records the rent, the social fund and the scholarships as delivered and the water treatment plant, the hiring preference and the ejido-run canteen and ore transport as not; by 2016 the rent had stopped as well, and the Agrarian Tribunal's resolution of 16 November 2016 valued the unbuilt water treatment plant at 5.5 million pesos while awarding the company the same sum for the blockade, so nothing changed hands.

cases.confidence_note: The court record is outside the complaint: a federal district court in La Laguna granted the ejido's amparo on 7 August 2014 and held that the withheld rent irreparably harmed the community, Proceso, a Mexican national magazine, reported the unpaid rent and the stalled agrarian case on 10 November 2016, and Excellon's own annual information form records the Agrarian Tribunal's resolution of 16 November 2016. The company's position is on the record and differs from the ejido's: Excellon states that it sued to terminate the contract, calls the 2012 blockade illegal, attributes the demonstrations to a campaign by competing unions to control its workforce, and says the water treatment plant depended on conditions the ejido never met, including a water use permit. The destruction of the camp rests on Red TDT, a Mexican human rights network, which names Excellon's director of operations, together with MiningWatch Canada's visit to the site on 3 December 2012; the criminal complaint over it produced no investigation, and no police report or court finding on the camp itself was opened here. The Mexican NCP found the issues not substantiated, which is a decision on the complaint and not a finding on the facts. On the location, Red TDT and MiningWatch Canada both place the Ejido La Sierrita de Galeana in Tlahualilo municipality; no document opened names the municipality the mine itself stands in, Excellon's annual information form puts the property about 45 km north of Torreon with a company warehouse in Bermejillo, and Red TDT records police from Mapimi municipality among those who tried to clear the protest camp on 29 August 2012.

cases.title: PT Nikomas Gemilang, Serang: the Yue Yuen shoe complex
cases.point: The PT Nikomas Gemilang shoe complex in eastern Serang, Banten, about 60 km from Jakarta. Besides shoe and chemical factories the site holds water treatment plants, offices, power plants, dormitories, canteens and a 70-bed polyclinic.

lenders.name: Pou Chen Corporation (Taiwan), through Yue Yuen (foreign owner and investor)
lenders.role: Owns the factory. Connor's 2002 report records PT Nikomas Gemilang as owned by the Pou Chen corporation, Nike's largest sport shoe supplier, which also owned large shoe factories in China and Vietnam. Merk's 2022 study records Nikomas as a subsidiary of Yue Yuen, the world's largest footwear manufacturer, and records that Yue Yuen has been active in Indonesia since 1993, when it invested about $100 million in the Nikomas complex. This investment is the outside link; the buyers' orders are not.

lenders.name: Nike, Inc. (United States) (foreign buyer, not the qualifying link)
lenders.role: Main customer of the factory and the respondent in the complaint. A buyer does not pass this map's link test on its own. Connor's 2001 report for Global Exchange asked Nike to send representatives to meet Nikomas workers and to commit to letting them organise without retribution, and to set up a confidential route for workers to report threats; his 2002 report says those requests had been ignored. Nike later investigated the unpaid overtime with the national SPN union, sending two teams including one undercover, and both concluded forced overtime was happening.

cases.conditions: No lender and no loan conditions; the outside money was the Taiwanese owner's investment in the site and the buyers' orders. The only conditions on the record are Nike's own code of conduct and its Fair Labour Association membership, which the US contact point cited when it closed the complaint on 27 May 2004.

companies.name: Pou Chen Corporation
companies.desc: Taiwanese shoe manufacturer, recorded by Connor in 2002 as Nike's largest sport shoe supplier and as the owner of several other large sport shoe factories in China and Vietnam, including the Yue Yuen complex at Dongguan with more than 40,000 workers. Merk records its Yue Yuen arm as the world's largest footwear manufacturer, with about 350,000 workers, founded in Taiwan in the late 1960s, taking orders from all the major sportswear brands.

companies.name: Nike, Inc.
companies.desc: American sportswear company. The Associated Press reported in July 2011 that Indonesia was Nike's third-largest manufacturing base, after China and Vietnam.

companies.name: PT Nikomas Gemilang
companies.role: The factory; named in the complaint as the company in violation
companies.desc: The Pou Chen group's largest Indonesian shoe plant, making footwear for Nike, Adidas, Puma, Asics, Saucony and K-Swiss: more than 24,000 workers in 2002 (Connor) and 68,000 to 80,000 by 2022, 75 to 80% of them women (Merk), which Merk calls the largest factory in Indonesia.

cases.community: Connor's 2002 report records more than 24,000 workers at the plant, making shoes for both Nike and adidas. Workers who organised a pay demonstration on 17 and 18 December 1999 were pushed out: one of them, Julianto, was taken into an office and told, in front of an Indonesian soldier, that he would be attacked by hired thugs if he did not stop organising, and was then approached repeatedly in the street by strangers warning that his life was in danger if he did not resign; another worker came home to find his house ransacked by a local gang. By April 2000 all twenty workers who had played a key part in organising the demonstration had resigned. Workers told Connor the factory had a history of employing Indonesian soldiers for security in the factory and preman, hired local thugs, to intimidate organisers, and that reporting problems got workers branded as troublemakers, mocked by supervisors or moved to harder and more dangerous sections. Jeroen Merk's 2022 field study found the same pattern two decades on: at least three national unions had tried and failed to set up branches since Connor's report, and local strongmen, jawara, were mobilised to protect the factory during the national wage protests of 2013. Merk records that the SPN branch at the plant regularly negotiates the collective agreement and does negotiate seniority, holiday benefits, severance pay and women's right to menstruation leave, but never negotiates wages, although most workers earn only the minimum wage. On the money, Merk records that in January 2012 the factory agreed to compensate 4,500 workers for close to 600,000 hours of unpaid overtime over two years, in a practice the activist Jim Keady calculated had run for 18 years; the agreement reached back only two years because Indonesian law allows redress only for the last two. Job applicants, Merk found, commonly paid recruiters roughly one to two months' wages. Asked about organising at the plant, Emelia Yanti of the union federation GSBI told him: "It is very, very difficult at this factory."
cases.suppression: On 21 March 2001 Rakhmat Suryadi, a union official at the factory, was attacked by a number of men with machetes in front of the plant on his way to work. He suffered head and leg wounds, needed 18 stitches in the back of his head, spent a week in hospital and could not work for a month. His attackers said nothing and made no attempt to rob him. The attack came a month after he had been quoted in the Indonesian newspaper Kompas describing labour abuses in Nike contract factories. Local unions and human rights organisations told Connor that several men were arrested over the attack and confessed, saying a local official had paid them. After the attack many workers who had been meeting to discuss their rights stopped doing so. Earlier, the twenty organisers of the December 1999 demonstration were forced out by threats of violence.
cases.outcome: The Clean Clothes Campaign, its Austrian partner and Global Exchange filed on 5 September 2002. The Austrian NCP declined the case for want of a link with Austria and passed it to the US NCP, which rejected it on 27 May 2004, saying the information available did not indicate that its involvement was needed and that Nike's conduct was being effectively addressed through other appropriate means, pointing to the company's participation in the Fair Labour Association. That is a decision on the complaint, not a finding on what happened in Serang. The parallel complaint against adidas, which also sourced from this factory, went to the German NCP and ended in September 2004 without agreement. The unpaid overtime was settled a decade later: the national board of the SPN took up the case over the heads of the factory's own union officials, Nike sent two investigating teams, one of them undercover, and both found forced overtime was happening; the factory then admitted the practice, adopted an eight-point programme including stopping production ten minutes before the end of a shift, and agreed to compensate 4,500 workers for close to 600,000 hours. Merk cites a BBC report of 12 January 2012 for the sum, about $1 million.
cases.whole: The plant grew through and after the dispute: from more than 24,000 workers in 2002 to 68,000 to 80,000 by 2022, 75 to 80% of them women, on a site Yue Yuen had been running since 1993, when it invested about $100 million in it. The Associated Press reported 140,000 workers at 14 of Nike's contract factories in Indonesia in July 2011; those figures sit in a fact box that names no source. What the complaint asked for did not arrive: Merk found no successful independent union branch at the factory in the twenty years after 2002, and the only documented payment to workers is the January 2012 overtime compensation, covering 4,500 workers and close to 600,000 hours, which reached back two years against a practice Keady calculated had run for 18, because Indonesian law allows redress only for the last two.

cases.confidence_note: The pattern of union suppression at this factory is recorded outside the complaint by Jeroen Merk's 2022 field study in the Journal fuer Entwicklungspolitik, based on interviews with national union officials and two focus groups of Nikomas workers. The January 2012 settlement is Merk's account, drawing on an SPN officer's study; the sum of about $1 million comes from a BBC report of 12 January 2012 which Merk cites and which was not opened here, so that one figure is given as Merk states it. The machete attack and the 1999 intimidation come from Timothy Connor's 2002 report, which is also the report the complaint was based on. Who ordered the attack on Rakhmat Suryadi is not established: Connor records that most of the workers interviewed suspected Nikomas managers, that arrested men said a local lurah paid them, that it is unclear whether the lurah was asked by anyone else, and that even if a factory was involved it may not have been Nikomas, since Suryadi had supported union activity at the nearby PT Spindo Mills as well. The Nikomas branch leader of the SPTSK union told Connor in January 2002 that wages and conditions at the plant were good and that there was no repression of union rights, which contradicted the confidential testimony of sixteen workers interviewed in July 2001 and January 2002. On the overtime, a senior Nikomas manager first denied the practice and the factory union's chairman wrote that the claims were incorrect, before the factory admitted it. No response from Nike or Pou Chen to the accounts of violence and intimidation was found in the sources opened. The Associated Press report of 2011 is cited only for Nike's Indonesian manufacturing base; the abuse it documents was at a Pou Chen plant in Sukabumi and at PT Amara Footwear, not at Nikomas.

cut.why: Fails test 1. TUV Rheinland India sold a social audit service to a BSCI member buyer; the complaint itself records that the audit was initiated by a BSCI member (ECCHR complaint of 7 July 2015, p. on audit report BL-18/12). The map's standing precedent (BRIEF13, BRIEF15, BRIEF17, CHECK13 and docs/HANDOFF.md) is that the outside party must have lent, invested, insured or set the loan condition, and that a foreign company which was only a contractor, supplier or buyer does not pass. A paid auditor is a service supplier: it put no money into the building, held no stake in Phantom Apparel Ltd and carried none of the loss when the building fell. Certification is not insurance, because the certifier transfers no financial risk onto itself. The harm (the 24 April 2013 collapse) is documented far outside the complaint and the timing overlaps, so tests 2 and 3 pass; test 1 is the one that fails. Keeping it would admit auditors, certifiers, consultants and ratings agencies as qualifying links, which is the same class the writer's own drops in this batch (Atlas Copco, Sandvik) and in batch 2 (Equinor, Total, TechnipFMC) excluded.

Fails test 1. adidas-Salomon was the buyer and nothing more: the Worker Rights Consortium's September 2004 assessment records that PT Panarub made athletic shoes exclusively for adidas-Salomon, and no document opened shows adidas or any other foreign company owning, lending to, insuring or investing in PT Panarub, which Connor's 2002 report and the WRC assessment treat as an Indonesian supplier. Under the same precedent that cut the auditor case above, a buyer does not pass. The harm is well recorded - the WRC's own factory assessment and the 2001 arrest, detention and acquittal of the union secretary Ngadinah Binti Abu Mawardi - so this is a test 1 cut, not a sourcing one. Note also that the assessment which made the card 'documented' was commissioned and paid for by the respondent, adidas, in January 2004, so it is not fully outside the company either.

corrections.was: No lender and no loan conditions; the outside money was the Taiwanese owner's investment and the buyers' orders. The only conditions on the record are Nike's own code of conduct and its Fair Labour Association membership, which the US NCP cited when it closed the complaint.
corrections.now: No lender and no loan conditions; the outside money was the Taiwanese owner's investment in the site and the buyers' orders. The only conditions on the record are Nike's own code of conduct and its Fair Labour Association membership, which the US contact point cited when it closed the complaint on 27 May 2004.

corrections.was: Nike and Pou Chen descriptions cited to Wikipedia; Nikomas given as "about 68,000 by 2022"
corrections.now: descriptions rewritten from Connor, Merk and the Associated Press; workforce given as Merk gives it, 68,000 to 80,000

corrections.was: the workers who organised a 2002 strike resigned under threat
corrections.now: the demonstration was on 17 and 18 December 1999 and the organisers had resigned by April 2000; Merk is describing Connor's account of that episode, not a 2002 strike

corrections.was: the dominant SPN union has never negotiated wages, according to the workers he interviewed
corrections.now: Merk records that the SPN branch regularly negotiates the collective agreement and does negotiate seniority, holiday benefits, severance pay and menstruation leave, but never wages

corrections.was: about $1 million in overtime owed to 4,500 workers, some 600,000 unpaid hours over two years, in a practice reported to have run for 18 years
corrections.now: the $1 million figure is Merk citing a BBC report of 12 January 2012 and is moved to the outcome with that attribution; Merk's own text gives 4,500 workers and close to 600,000 hours over two years, with the two-year limit set by Indonesian law and the 18 years being Jim Keady's calculation

corrections.was: the US NCP, which closed it (no date); "The unpaid overtime was settled a decade later, in January 2012, for about $1 million covering 4,500 workers."
corrections.now: closure dated 27 May 2004; the settlement account expanded from Merk (SPN national board, Nike's two investigating teams, the factory's admission and eight-point programme) with the $1 million attributed to the BBC report Merk cites

corrections.was: Nike had 140,000 workers at 14 contract factories in Indonesia by 2011, by the figures its own monitoring supplied to the Associated Press
corrections.now: the figures appear in an Associated Press fact box that names no source; nothing on the page attributes them to Nike's own monitoring

corrections.was: included https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pou_Chen and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc.
corrections.now: both removed; Connor and Merk carry the ownership and group facts the Wikipedia entries were used for

corrections.was: the January 2012 overtime settlement he reports was first reported by the BBC; that BBC report was not opened here, so the figures are given as Merk states them
corrections.now: narrowed: only the $1 million sum comes from the BBC report Merk cites; the 4,500 workers and close to 600,000 hours are Merk's own text. Also added the company-side denials and then admission, and dropped the unverified description of the journal as peer-reviewed.
